title: English in Global Media
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about who tells the world its news -- how English-language media shapes global narratives, the theory of media imperialism, and the 'CNN effect' that can move governments.

content.content:
## English and the Global News Landscape

When a major event happens anywhere in the world, the first international coverage almost always arrives in English. Whether it is a natural disaster in Southeast Asia, a political crisis in South America, or a scientific breakthrough in Europe, English-language news agencies are typically the first to broadcast the story to a global audience.

This dominance is no accident. It is the product of historical power, economic resources, and technological infrastructure that has placed English at the centre of the world's information systems. Organisations like the BBC, CNN, Reuters, and the Associated Press have built vast networks of correspondents, studios, and digital platforms reaching billions of people daily. But this raises important questions. When most international news is produced in English, by English-speaking organisations, whose perspectives are prioritized? Which stories get told, and which are left out? In this chapter we explore the role of English in global media, the theory of media imperialism, and the power dynamics embedded in how the world receives its news.

## Media Imperialism and the Big News Agencies

**Media imperialism** is a theory describing how dominant nations -- particularly English-speaking Western countries -- exert disproportionate influence over global media flows. Its core principles are a **one-way flow** of information from the Global North to the Global South, **cultural dominance** spreading the values of media-producing nations, **structural inequality** because developing nations lack the resources to compete, and **language gatekeeping** where English acts as a filter for global news. Key thinkers include Herbert Schiller (who argued in 1969 that American media served American interests), Oliver Boyd-Barrett (who coined "media imperialism" in 1977), and Daya Thussu. But there are counter-arguments too: audiences are not passive recipients but interpret media through local frameworks; regional powerhouses like Al Jazeera and CGTN challenge Western dominance; digital platforms let alternative voices reach global audiences; and hybridization occurs as global content is adapted locally.

The backbone of English-language news is formed by a handful of organisations. The **BBC World Service** (founded 1932) reaches 489 million people weekly and is known for perceived impartiality. **CNN International** (founded 1985) is available in over 200 countries and gave rise to the "CNN effect." **Reuters** (founded 1851) is one of the "Big Three" wire agencies, supplying news to thousands of outlets. The **Associated Press** (founded 1846) is the oldest news agency in the world. And **Agence France-Presse** (founded 1835) provides a European perspective. To see how framing shapes coverage, imagine the BBC and Al Jazeera reporting the same Middle East conflict: the BBC might frame it within Western foreign-policy concerns and use diplomatic language, while Al Jazeera might centre voices from the affected region and emphasize humanitarian consequences. Both practise professional journalism, but their framing, source selection, and assumed audience shape the story. Neither is "neutral" -- which is why media literacy requires comparing multiple sources.

options.text: How all countries produce equal amounts of news
How news travels only within one country
How media has no effect on culture
How dominant English-speaking nations exert disproportionate influence over global media flows

questions.solution: Media imperialism describes a largely one-way flow of news and perspectives from powerful Western nations to the rest of the world, with English as a key gatekeeper.

questions.task: Which is a counter-argument to media imperialism?

options.text: Regional powerhouses like Al Jazeera and CGTN challenge Western dominance
Audiences accept all media completely passively
Only Western media exists
Digital platforms silence all alternative voices

questions.solution: Counter-arguments note that audiences interpret media actively, regional outlets like Al Jazeera challenge Western dominance, and digital platforms enable alternative voices.

questions.task: What does comparing BBC and Al Jazeera coverage reveal?

options.text: That one outlet always lies and the other always tells the truth
That framing, source selection, and assumed audience shape every story -- no outlet is fully neutral
That both produce identical coverage
That neutral coverage is easy to find

questions.solution: Both outlets practise professional journalism, but their framing and source choices shape the story differently. Neither is absolutely neutral, so media literacy requires comparing sources.

questions.solution: Reuters is one of the 'Big Three' wire agencies, alongside the Associated Press (AP) and Agence France-Presse (AFP), supplying news to thousands of outlets worldwide.

content.content:
## The CNN Effect and Language Gatekeeping

One of the most striking ideas in media studies is the **CNN effect** -- the notion that live, 24-hour English-language news coverage can influence government policy. The classic case is the 1992 Somalia crisis. CNN broadcast harrowing footage of famine and civil war in Mogadishu; public outrage grew as the images circulated; President George H.W. Bush authorized Operation Restore Hope; and US Marines landed on Somali beaches in December 1992, greeted by CNN cameras. The CNN effect suggests media coverage drove policy -- though critics argue the government was already planning intervention and used the coverage to build support. The case shows both the power of English-language media to set the global agenda and its danger: when the cameras left Somalia, so did international attention. Today, social media amplifies the CNN effect, with smartphone footage reaching millions before traditional media reports -- though "compassion fatigue" may reduce the effect over time.

Underlying all of this is **gatekeeping** -- the process by which information is filtered, shaped, and selected before reaching audiences. When English functions as the dominant language of international news, it becomes a powerful gatekeeper. Stories must be deemed "newsworthy" by English-language editors to reach international audiences; local events in non-English-speaking countries may go unreported unless they affect English-speaking nations; translation inevitably changes nuance; and sources who speak English are more likely to be quoted. The consequences include **Anglophone bias** (events in English-speaking countries get disproportionate coverage), **elite focus** (English-speaking elites become the default sources), **narrative simplification**, and **terminology power** (English terms like "terrorism" or "freedom fighter" frame how issues are understood globally). But English dominance is being challenged -- by regional media outlets like Al Jazeera, CGTN, RT, and NHK World; by multilingual digital platforms and automatic translation; and by citizen journalism in local languages reaching global audiences through social media.

options.text: placeholder
The effect of watching too much television
A type of camera technology
The way CNN reduces its own ratings
The idea that live, 24-hour news coverage can influence government policy

questions.solution: The CNN effect is the idea that live, round-the-clock news coverage can shape government policy and public opinion, as suggested by the 1992 Somalia intervention.

options.text: The process by which information is filtered, shaped, and selected before reaching audiences
Guarding the entrance to a TV studio
Translating all news into Latin
Banning all foreign news

questions.solution: Gatekeeping is the filtering and selection of information before it reaches audiences. When English dominates international news, it becomes a powerful gatekeeper of what the world sees.

questions.task: What is 'Anglophone bias' in global news?

options.text: A preference for non-English news
Events in English-speaking countries receive disproportionate coverage
The banning of English news
Equal coverage of all countries

questions.solution: Anglophone bias means events in English-speaking countries receive disproportionate coverage, while local events elsewhere may go unreported unless they affect English-speaking nations.

questions.task: How is English dominance in global media being challenged?

options.text: By banning all non-English media
By making English the only legal language
By regional outlets like Al Jazeera, digital platforms, and citizen journalism in local languages
It is not being challenged at all

questions.solution: English dominance is challenged by regional media powerhouses (Al Jazeera, CGTN, RT), multilingual digital platforms, automatic translation, and citizen journalism in local languages.

content.content:
## Summary

English-language media organisations dominate global information flows, creating a largely one-way stream of news and perspectives from powerful Western nations -- the basis of the theory of **media imperialism**. The major players -- the **BBC**, **CNN**, **Reuters**, **AP**, and **AFP** -- shape how billions understand world events through their framing, source selection, and editorial choices, as a comparison of BBC and Al Jazeera coverage reveals. The **CNN effect** shows how live English-language coverage can influence government policy, as in the 1992 Somalia crisis. **Gatekeeping** means English acts as a filter, producing Anglophone bias, elite focus, and terminology power. Yet this dominance is increasingly challenged by regional outlets, digital platforms, and citizen journalism -- creating a more diverse but also more fragmented global media landscape.
